title: Ports: Many Doors, One Address
about: How one address can run many services at once.

cards.prompt:
One [[server]] at `198.51.100.10` runs a website, an email service and a game, all at once, all on one [[IP address]].

A [[packet]] arrives for `198.51.100.10`. The address got it to the right computer. What else does the packet need so it reaches the right **program**?

options.text: A number that says which program on that computer it's for
Every program gets a copy and ignores whatever isn't meant for it
options.nudge: Copying every packet to every program would be slow, and anyone could read anyone's data. There's a neater way to point it at one program.

options.text: Nothing: each program has its own IP address on that computer
options.nudge: Here all three programs share the one IP address, `198.51.100.10`. So the address alone can't pick between them.

options.text: The server hands it to whichever program is least busy right now
options.nudge: A game can't make sense of an email. The packet has to say where it belongs, not land wherever there's room.

cards.explanation: Every packet also carries a number that picks the program: a **port**. The IP address gets it to the right computer, and the port gets it to the right program. Programs don't each get their own address here, they don't share copies, and the server never guesses.
cards.hint: The IP address is the same for all three programs. So something else in the packet has to tell them apart.

cards.title: Ports are like apartment numbers
cards.body:
Think of an apartment building. The street address gets a letter to the **building**, and the apartment number gets it to the right **door**.

The [[IP address]] is the building, and a **port** is the door. Each program **listens** on its own port. Websites use port `80`, and secure websites ([[HTTPS]]) use `443`. Together: `198.51.100.10:443`.

options.text: Port 443: the door for the secure website program
A fifth octet, added to the IP address to make it longer
options.nudge: An IPv4 address always has exactly four octets. The colon marks the start of something separate from the address.

options.text: The packet is allowed to travel through up to 443 routers
options.nudge: Routers get the packet to the right computer. The number after the colon is about what happens once it's there.

options.text: The server promises to answer within 443 milliseconds
options.nudge: Nothing in an address measures time. Think about which program on the server the packet should reach.

cards.explanation: The part after the colon is the **port**. 443 is the standard port for secure websites ([[HTTPS]]), so this means "the secure website program at 198.51.100.10". It isn't part of the IP address, which always has exactly four octets, and it has nothing to do with routers or timing.
cards.hint: Think of the apartment building: the IP address is the building. What does the number after the colon pick out?

cards.prompt:
Your side of a conversation needs a [[port]] too, so replies reach the right app. Your laptop picks a temporary one, usually a high number like `51544`.

On Windows, `netstat -n` lists connections. **Local Address** is your laptop's end; **Foreign Address** is the other end. Run it and find which port on the [[server]] `198.51.100.10` this laptop is connected to.
cards.intro:
Microsoft Windows [simulated Command Prompt]
Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.output:
Active Connections

  Proto  Local Address          Foreign Address        State
  TCP    192.168.1.42:51544     198.51.100.10:443      ESTABLISHED
  TCP    192.168.1.42:51547     203.0.113.80:80        ESTABLISHED

success.question: Which port on 198.51.100.10 is the laptop connected to?

cards.explanation: The first line's **Foreign Address** is `198.51.100.10:443`, so it's port **443**: a secure website. `51544` is the laptop's own temporary port, under **Local Address**. The second line is a plain website on port 80, and it has a different temporary port (`51547`), so the two replies never get mixed up.
cards.hint: Run `netstat -n`, find the line with `198.51.100.10`, and look at the number after its colon under **Foreign Address**.
cards.nudge: **Local Address** is your laptop's own end. The server's port is in the **Foreign Address** column, after the colon.

cards.prompt:
Your home [[router]] shares one [[public address]] using **NAT**. Ports are how it keeps replies apart: it swaps your laptop's private address and port for its public address and a port it picks, and writes the pair in its **NAT table**.

Put the steps in order.

items.label: The router changes the sender to 203.0.113.7:40001 and adds it to its NAT table
The router finds port 40001 in its table and passes the reply to 192.168.1.20:51000

cards.explanation: The router rewrites the sender on the way **out** and records it. The server only ever sees `203.0.113.7:40001`, so it replies there. The router then uses the port number to look up which device the reply belongs to.
cards.hint: Follow one [[packet]] out and its reply back in. The router has to write something in its table before it can look it up.
cards.nudge: The server only ever sees the router's public address and port. So what must happen before the server can reply there?

cards.prompt:
The [[router]]'s [[NAT]] table says:

- `203.0.113.7:40001` → `192.168.1.20:51000`
- `203.0.113.7:40002` → `192.168.1.21:51000`

A reply arrives for `203.0.113.7:40002`. Which device gets it? Type the **last number** of its [[private address]].
cards.explanation: Port **40002** maps to `192.168.1.21:51000`, so the device ending in **21** gets it. Both laptops happened to use port 51000, but the router gave them different public ports, so their replies never get mixed up.
cards.hint: Match the full public address and [[port]] of the reply to a line in the table, then read the private address on the right.
cards.nudge: Both laptops use port 51000, so that won't tell them apart. Look at the router's public port in the reply to pick the right line.

cards.prompt: Two laptops at home both happen to use port **51000** to reach the same website. How does the [[router]] keep their replies apart?

options.text: It gives each one a different public port, like 40001 and 40002
It can't, so one laptop's connection fails until the other finishes
options.nudge: Lots of devices share one home router without problems. Think about what the router gets to choose when it rewrites the sender.

options.text: It sends every reply to both laptops and lets them sort it out
options.nudge: The NAT table exists so each reply goes to exactly one device. What could make the two replies look different when they arrive?

options.text: The server puts each laptop's private address in its reply
options.nudge: The server never sees the private addresses: the router swaps them out on the way. The answer lies in the router's own table.

cards.explanation: The router picks a **different public port** for each conversation, so the replies arrive on different ports and its NAT table says which laptop each one belongs to. Nothing fails, nothing is sent to both, and the server never even learns the private addresses.
cards.hint: Think about the [[NAT]] table. The router picks the public port for each conversation, so what could it do differently for each laptop?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The [[IP address]] finds the computer; the **port** finds the program.
- Websites use port 80; secure websites use 443.
- Your router's **NAT table** uses ports to route each reply home.

Next: two ways to deliver data, TCP and UDP.
